strengths: The core idea—dual-scale parameterization combined with a Sinkhorn-Knopp-style balancing of row and column standard deviations—is mathematically intuitive, elegant, and computationally lightweight.

The method requires no calibration data and treats each linear layer independently, avoiding cross-layer interdependencies (such as those introduced by Hadamard or learned rotation matrices) and facilitating out-of-the-box application to diverse architectures.

Quantization overhead is exceptionally low; empirical results indicate runtime is only ~1.1x of naive RTN, substantially faster than HQQ (~2.3x) and calibration-based methods like GPTQ and AWQ (>30x).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families and scales, including recent dense and MoE models (Qwen3, Llama 2/3, DeepSeek-V2.5, and DeepSeek-V3), evaluating perplexity, task flip rates, and reasoning benchmarks (AIME).
Good versatility and composability: SINQ demonstrates strong synergy when paired with non-uniform quantization levels (e.g., NF4) as well as data-driven calibration (A-SINQ).
weaknesses: Lack of actual wall-clock inference latency measurements or dedicated kernel implementations: Although the paper shows that the column scale can be folded into activation scaling (Eq. 6), no benchmarks on real GPU inference speed (e.g., via custom Triton or CUDA/Marlin kernels) are provided to verify memory-bandwidth and compute efficiency in practical deployment.

Heuristic convergence properties: Unlike classical Sinkhorn-Knopp for nonnegative matrices, normalizing standard deviations with min-clipping and early stopping lacks formal convergence guarantees or theoretical error bounds under general weight distributions.

Evaluation is predominantly focused on 4-bit and 3-bit regimes; exploring extreme quantization (such as 2-bit or 2.5-bit average precision) would help clarify the limits of dual-scaling without explicit Hessian or rotation compensation.
Visual presentation in Figures 3 and 4 could be improved, as the axis labels, legends, and plotted curves are quite small and difficult to read without significant zoom.

strengths: Practical and computationally lightweight approach: SINQ leverages a modified Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration to alternate row and column variance normalization, introducing minimal overhead (only ~1.09x runtime over standard RTN, substantially faster than HQQ at ~2.3x and calibration-based methods at >30x).

Architecture-agnostic and localized: Unlike rotational PTQ methods (e.g., QuaRot, SpinQuant) that require cross-layer coordinate transforms and can be cumbersome to implement on non-standard architectures, SINQ quantizes each linear layer independently. This makes it cleanly compatible with complex architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA).

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is benchmarked across an extensive selection of modern architectures and scales (Qwen3 family from 0.6B to 235B MoE, DeepSeek-V2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Llama 2/3), demonstrating consistent gains in perplexity, flip rates, and reasoning accuracy (AIME) over uncalibrated baselines.

Flexibility and orthogonality: The paper demonstrates that dual-scaling can be easily adapted to non-uniform quantization grids (NF4) and combined synergistically with activation-aware calibration (AWQ / A-SINQ).
weaknesses: Lack of inference runtime / latency evaluation: While Section 2.3 discusses how the column-wise scale vector can be folded into post-GEMM activation scaling for 1D tiling, the paper does not report actual inference latency or kernel-level throughput (e.g., via Triton or CUDA kernels). Demonstrating that the additional element-wise scaling does not degrade generation speed on GPU/NPU hardware is crucial for deployment.

Absence of theoretical convergence analysis: Algorithm 1 alternates scaling by standard deviations with clipping/flooring. While standard Sinkhorn-Knopp on non-negative matrices enjoys well-understood convergence properties to doubly stochastic matrices, variance/standard-deviation normalization does not trivially inherit these guarantees. The paper lacks formal analysis or bounds regarding the convergence or stability of this heuristic.

Scope limited to weight-only quantization: Although the introduction discusses compute-bound regimes and activation quantization, the experimental validation is restricted entirely to weight-only quantization (W3A16, W4A16). Evaluating whether dual-scaling can assist under low-precision activation regimes (e.g., W8A8 or W4A4) remains unaddressed.

Incomplete presentation details: There are missing placeholders in the manuscript (e.g., the code repository URL is left blank in the abstract: 'available at .'), and Figure 1 contains tiny, low-resolution schematic text.

strengths: Simple and elegant concept: The proposed dual-scaling parameterization and Sinkhorn-style standard deviation balancing address weight outliers effectively without needing cross-layer coordinate transformations (e.g., Hadamard rotations) or calibration datasets.

Very fast quantization execution: Because the method operates on individual weight matrices via a few iterations of standard deviation normalization, quantization runtime is only ~1.09x of basic RTN, significantly outperforming HQQ and calibrated methods like AWQ and GPTQ.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate across a diverse set of model architectures and scales (dense LLaMA models, Qwen models from 1.7B to 235B, DeepSeek-V2.5 and V3 MoE with MLA), reporting perplexity (WikiText2, C4), QA flip rates, and reasoning performance (AIME).
Versatility and composability: SINQ demonstrates clean composability with non-uniform quantization formats (NF4) as well as data-driven calibration methods (A-SINQ with AWQ).
weaknesses: Algorithmic error in Algorithm 1: The pseudocode reassigns the scale vectors \sigma_0 and \sigma_1 in each iteration of the loop without accumulating them. In step 10, returning s \odot \sigma_1 and \sigma_0 would only apply the final iteration's scaling rather than the product over all iterations, failing to reconstruct the scaled weights. The broadcasting semantics (e.g., dividing W by \sigma_1 without unsqueezing) are also informal and would fail in standard matrix libraries.

No inference latency or kernel benchmarks: While Section 2.3 shows that 1D tiling allows the column scale \vec{t} to be folded into output activation scaling (similar to AWQ), the paper only reports offline quantization time and theoretical model memory. It lacks actual end-to-end inference latency or low-precision GEMM throughput measurements on real accelerator hardware.

Lack of theoretical convergence analysis: Unlike classical Sinkhorn-Knopp on non-negative matrices which has established convergence guarantees, alternating standard deviation division with clipping is an empirical heuristic. The paper provides no theoretical analysis regarding convergence conditions, bounds, or potential oscillatory behavior.

Presentation oversights: The code repository URL in the abstract is missing ('available at .'). In addition, some plots (such as Figure 2c and 2f) have cluttered text and axes that are difficult to read.

strengths: Compelling conceptual insight: The observation that column-wise weight standard deviations correlate with incoming activation magnitudes (due to the dynamics of Adam updates) provides an elegant explanation for why calibration-free methods can approximate activation-aware scaling.

Fast and lightweight method: The proposed alternating normalization algorithm is remarkably fast (incurring only ~1.1× the runtime of naive RTN, significantly faster than HQQ and calibrated methods like AWQ/GPTQ) and architecture-agnostic without cross-layer coupling.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation: The paper evaluates across diverse model families (Qwen, Llama 2/3, Phi-2/3/4, DeepSeek-V2.5/V3), scales (from 0.6B to 685B), and architectures (dense, MoE, and MLA). It reports both language modeling perplexities (WikiText-2, C4) and downstream performance (flip rates, accuracy, reasoning benchmarks like AIME).

Practical deployment considerations: The paper addresses inference kernel compatibility, measures end-to-end decode throughput in SGLang and llama.cpp, and provides a viable 'no-overhead' absorption strategy for preceding layers.
weaknesses: Heuristic connection to Sinkhorn-Knopp: While framed as a 'Sinkhorn-Knopp-style' algorithm, Algorithm 1 is essentially an alternating heuristic balancing of standard deviations in log-space with step clamping. Unlike standard Sinkhorn scaling on non-negative matrices to achieve doubly stochastic forms, there are no formal convergence guarantees or proofs provided for this procedure.

Heuristic derivation of the inverse-root relationship: The analytical link between weight standard deviation and input scale (Eq. 4: s_W ∝ 1 / sqrt(|s_x|)) is demonstrated only on a toy single-layer linear model with Gaussian inputs and Adam optimizer. A more rigorous theoretical analysis characterizing this behavior across multi-layer non-linear transformers would strengthen the foundation.

Sensitivity and hyperparameter analysis: Algorithm 1 relies on multiple hyperparameters (number of iterations K, step sizes s_min and s_max, target variance tau). The manuscript lacks an ablation or sensitivity analysis detailing how sensitive quantization quality is to these parameters across different layer types.

Trade-offs in the no-overhead variant: In modern architectures where layers share inputs (e.g., Q, K, V projections or Gate and Up projections), absorbing scales requires tying/sharing scales across these matrices, which leads to noticeable perplexity degradation compared to unconstrained dual-scaling (as shown in Table 8).

strengths: Insightful Connection Between Training Dynamics and Activation Scales: The paper presents a compelling empirical finding that column-wise weight standard deviations inversely correlate with input activation magnitudes due to Adam optimization dynamics. This provides a principled explanation for why calibration-free pseudo-activation scaling is possible without calibration datasets.

Well-Motivated Sinkhorn Normalization Formulation: The proposed dual-scaling and dampened log-space Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration (Algorithm 1) directly tackles the problem of row-wise kurtosis and outlier amplification that naive column scaling causes, balancing row and column variances effectively.

Near-Zero Quantization Overhead: SINQ requires only ~1.1× the runtime of naive RTN, making it significantly faster than optimization-based calibration-free methods like HQQ (>2×) and orders of magnitude faster than calibrated methods like AWQ (>30×) or GPTQ (>60×).

Extensive and Rigorous Empirical Evaluation: Experiments span modern and diverse LLM architectures (Qwen3 dense and MoE models up to 235B, DeepSeek-V2.5/V3 with MLA, Llama-2/3, and Phi family). Results thoroughly cover perplexity (WikiText2, C4), flip rates across reasoning and QA tasks (HellaSwag, PIQA, MMLU, AIME), and practical inference throughput in SGLang and llama.cpp/GGUF.
Modularity and Versatility: SINQ can readily combine with non-uniform formats (e.g., NF4) and calibrated algorithms (AWQ to form ASINQ), consistently improving or matching strong baselines.
weaknesses: Heuristic Derivation of the Scale Relationship: While the observation $\vec{s}_W \propto 1/\sqrt{|\vec{s}_x|}$ in Eq. (4) is intuitive and empirically supported on a single linear layer under Adam, the paper lacks a more rigorous theoretical treatment of how this relationship survives deep transformer features like RMSNorm/LayerNorm, residual streams, and non-linear gating (e.g., SwiGLU).

Lack of Convergence and Hyperparameter Analysis for Algorithm 1: Algorithm 1 introduces dampening, clamping thresholds ($s_{\min}, s_{\max}$), and a heuristic matrix imbalance snapshot, but the paper does not provide an ablation or sensitivity study for these hyperparameters, nor formal convergence guarantees for the modified Sinkhorn iteration.

Clarification Needed on Group-Wise Tiling vs. Global Scales: Section 2.1.2 describes how per-tile scales and global column scales $\vec{t}$ interact, but the exact hardware execution and tensor layout implications when combining group-wise shift/scale tiling with per-channel input scaling $\vec{t}$ could be discussed with greater clarity in the main text.

Diminishing Margins in Calibrated Settings: While calibration-free SINQ significantly beats calibration-free baselines, when combined with calibration (A-SINQ vs. AWQ in Table 2 and Table 4), the performance delta in 4-bit quantization on larger models (e.g., Qwen3-14B/32B) is sometimes marginal (e.g., C4 perplexity 10.96 vs. 10.93).

strengths: Novel and insightful observation: The discovery that weight column standard deviations in pre-trained LLMs correlate inversely with input activation magnitudes allows for calibration-free, pseudo-activation-aware quantization without requiring calibration datasets.

Well-motivated algorithm: The Sinkhorn-Knopp-inspired balancing procedure elegantly addresses the issue of row-wise outlier amplification and kurtosis explosion that arises from naive column-wise scaling.

Negligible computational and quantization overhead: The quantization process requires only ~1.1x the compute of round-to-nearest (RTN), outperforming HQQ and calibrated methods by large margins, while runtime inference overhead is negligible (~1-2%) or zero when scales are absorbed into preceding layers.

Extensive and thorough empirical validation: Experiments span a wide range of architectures and model scales (from small models up to DeepSeek-V3 685B and Qwen3-235B MoE), covering perplexity benchmarks, flip rates on multiple-choice QA, reasoning evaluations (AIME), and real deployment frameworks (llama.cpp, SGLang).
Orthogonality and composability: The approach is shown to synergize effectively with non-uniform quantization formats (NF4) as well as data-driven calibration techniques (AWQ, yielding A-SINQ).
weaknesses: Heuristic justification of optimizer dynamics: While the relationship in Eq. (4) between weight standard deviation and input scale is demonstrated empirically and on a single-layer toy model, a rigorous theoretical analysis explaining how this persists across deep transformer architectures with RMSNorm/LayerNorm and attention mechanisms is lacking.

Clarity on group-wise tiling interaction: The paper quantizes models with group size 64, but Algorithm 1 describes the matrix normalization over the full $m \times n$ matrix $W$. A clearer mathematical description of how global dual scales $\vec{s}, \vec{t}$ interact with block/tile-level scales and shifts in Eq. (3) would improve technical clarity.

Trade-offs in the no-overhead variant: Absorbing input scales $\vec{t}$ into previous layers requires parameter sharing when multiple layers share inputs (such as Q/K/V projections and Gate/Up projections in SwiGLU), which introduces a minor quality trade-off that could be analyzed more deeply.

Limited evaluation on low-precision activation quantization: The paper focuses predominantly on weight-only quantization (W4A16 and W3A16), leaving the potential and limitations of SINQ for joint low-precision weight-activation settings (e.g., W4A4 or W8A8) largely unexplored.
